Acura Recalls ZDX Electric Crossover for Potential Loss of Brake Pressure
7 photos
Photo: Acura
A zero-emission crossover with GM underpinnings, the Acura ZDX was discontinued after the 2025 model year due to pitiful demand in the US market, a problem exacerbated by expiring federal incentives. Even though it's no longer produced, the Acura-branded model has been hit with a recall that affects all-wheel-drive specifications delivered for MY24 in the US market.
26V7350 is what the safety boffins at the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration call this campaign, which comprises 14,648 vehicles. The safety concern here stems from the electric brake control module. According to American Honda Motor, the EBCM software can miscalculate the vehicle's reference speed.
When this happens, the subject module may command an inappropriate reduction in brake pressure, compromising the braking performance of the affected vehicles. The miscalculation apparently occurs in very specific conditions. To the point, when any sort of wheel slip and light braking occur together with driving over a disturbance in the road.
American Honda Motor also notes a brake pedal that is either released or reapplied in the process. On high-friction surfaces, the iffy software interprets the resulting data as evidence of excessive slip. This, in turn, prompts the subject module to reduce brake pressure, reducing brake capability without any warning.
General Motors is identified in the recall documentation as the manufacturer of the suspect vehicles and the supplier of the brake control module software, which is split between no fewer than nine part numbers by American Honda Motor. Suspect production dates range from December 19, 2023, through January 22, 2025.
Photo: Acura Spring Hill, Tennessee, served as the home of the ZDX, whose BEV3 platform is shared with the Cadillac Lyriq, Honda Prologue, and Chevrolet Blazer EV . Rear-wheel drive by nature yet all-wheel drive by choice, the ZDX was never a big seller in the United States market. Only 109 units were delivered so far this year, 12,005 in 2025, and 7,391 in 2024, making it a bit of a commercial blunder.
As noted earlier, only dual-motor vehicles feature the suspect EBCM software. Honda first determined that such a defect exists in August 2024, resulting in recall 24V614. More than two years later, General Motors supplied additional information that forced the Japanese automaker to recall the ZDX yet again.
Thankfully for both customers and American Honda Motor's legal department, no injuries potentially associated with the described condition have been reported thus far. Even so, a temporary reduction in braking pressure is nothing to scoff at when the subject vehicle weighs 5,904 pounds (2,678 kilograms) at the very least. The performance-oriented Type S is listed with 6,052 lbs (2,745 kgs).
Customers who have accepted OTA terms and conditions will receive the updated EBCM software over the air. Everyone else can arrange a free-of-charge update at the Acura dealership of their liking. The new software package includes a revised calibration that corrects the false wheel slippage detection condition.
Customers will be notified by first-class mail no later than December 14, 2026. In the meantime, customers may check if their ZDXs need the update by running the 17-character VIN on the NHTSA's website.
